The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg is the RMS Titanic.

To understand blockchain technology, imagine a massive, shared notebook that is distributed among thousands of people instead of being kept in a single office. In a traditional system, like a bank's ledger, one central authority keeps the record. If that central record is altered or lost, the data can be compromised.

In the blockchain analogy, every person in the network holds an identical copy of this notebook. When a new transaction occurs, it is written into a "page" (or block) of the notebook. Before this page is added to the chain, everyone checks the math to ensure the transaction is valid. Once verified, the page is sealed with a unique digital lock (a cryptographic hash) and added to the chain. Because every copy of the notebook is updated simultaneously, no single person can secretly change a past entry without everyone else noticing and rejecting the change. This collective verification and distributed storage make the system extremely secure and trustworthy, as it relies on consensus rather than a single point of control.
